To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
‘The survival of cerebellar granules cells from mice, but not from rats, is independent of elevated potassium‐ion concentration in the culture medium.’

the effects of high K+ on the survival of cerebellar granulocytes are species specific, i.e. mouse cerebellar cells survive well in the presence of high K+ whereas rat granule cells require high K+ for their survival.
mouse cerebellar neurons, like rat cerebellar neurons but unlike most other neurons in vitro, require depolarization for survival.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms underlying the survival of cultured neurons.
the study of the mechanisms of neuronal survival and differentiation in culture.
the study of the survival requirements and biochemical differentiation of mouse and rat cerebelar granule cells in culture.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the survival of mouse cerebellar cells in culture does not depend upon K+‐induction of membrane depolarization.

the survival of mouse and rat cerebel­lar granule cells in vitro is promoted by K+‐induc­ed membrane depolarization in the rat, whereas the survival of mouse granule cells is independent of K+‐evoked depolarization.
K+‐inducible membrane depolarization is not required for the survival of cerebellar granules cells in vitro, but that it is required for biochemical differentiation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

K+‐inducible membrane depolarization is a prerequisite for the survival of cerebellar granular cells, but the biochemical parameters that are induced by K+‐induction are not essential for the survival of the cells.
the K+‐inducible biochemical differentiation of cerebellar granules is not a sufficient condition for the survival of these neurons.
rat cerebellar cells are more sensitive to K+ deprivation than mouse cerebellar cells, and that mouse granule cells are more sensitive than rat granule cells to K+ deprivation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the survival of mouse cerebellar cells is not dependent of high extracellular K+, which is in stark contrast to the survival of rat cerebellar cells.
the survival of cultured mouse granule cells is promoted by ‘low’ as well as by ‘high’ K+, while the survival of rat cells is dependent on ‘high’ K+.
mouse granule cells do not develop a K+‐induce membrane depolarization requirement for survival, in contrast to rat granule cells.
